title: Leo and Sofia Tolstoy: A Marriage That Made and Broke
text:
In September 1862, Leo Tolstoy, thirty-four, married Sofia Behrs, eighteen. Before the wedding he gave her his diaries to read, with their record of his past affairs, believing that honesty required it. She was deeply shocked and never quite forgot.

The early years of the marriage were productive. Sofia ran the estate at Yasnaya Polyana, bore thirteen children, of whom several died young, and became her husband's indispensable assistant. She copied out the manuscripts of War and Peace by hand, deciphering his crowded corrections, again and again, by candlelight. Anna Karenina followed.

From around 1880, Tolstoy underwent a religious crisis. He began preaching simplicity, chastity and the renunciation of property, and wanted to give up the copyrights on his works. Sofia, who had to provide for the family, fought him. His disciple Vladimir Chertkov gained more and more influence over him, and Sofia grew jealous and desperate. Both kept diaries, and each read the other's, which made things worse.

In 1910 Tolstoy signed a secret will leaving his copyrights to the public. In the night of 28 October, at eighty-two, he slipped out of the house and left. He fell ill on the train and died at the small station of Astapovo. Sofia hurried there, but she was kept from his bedside until he was no longer conscious.
lesson: A partnership that produced great work can still collapse if each partner stops trying to understand the other. Honesty without care can wound as deeply as lies.
people: Leo Tolstoy, Sofia Tolstaya, Vladimir Chertkov
source: The Diaries of Sofia Tolstoy, trans. Cathy Porter (1985); Tolstoy's diaries; A. N. Wilson, Tolstoy (1988)
